utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I thought it prudent to raise the issue of order of witnesses and associated matters before the witness came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. It appears that the accused has some difficulties with his microphone. Yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand that Jelic will be returning this morning. Indeed, I was approached to check that I understood that to be the position and was happy about it, and indeed I am. Can I possibly ask us to go into private session just for a minute or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may commence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We left off last week when we looked at the list of persons killed in Kacanik, which is Kotlina and Slatina, and you said something about that. You said that in view of the fact that they were all men and of a certain age, that you assumed that they must have been members of the KLA, but of course we cannot establish that just on that basis. Now, I'd like to have a document placed on the overhead projector which I have -- or, rather, received in May this year from Mr. Nice -- or, rather, my associates received the document from him. It's a very short one. So I'll read out what it says. It's in English. But may it be placed on the overhead projector so that we can focus on the last portion of the page. The upper part isn't that important. Do we have it on the overhead projector now? This is what it says at the bottom. I'll read it out in English and you'll hear the interpreter: "[In English] On 17 September 1999, OTP investigator Malvin Dagsland was informed by residents of the village of Kotlina -- was informed by residents of the village of Kotlina, municipality of Kacanik --" [Interpretation] I didn't hear the interpretation, that this person was informed by the residents of the village of Kotlina. That's what it says: "[In English] ... municipality of Kacanik ... that 12 of the persons whose bodies were found in the wells in Kotlina, following the attack on the village of 21 [sic] of March 1999, were KLA soldiers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: 24th of March, 1999, yes, were KLA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, what did you know about this event?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 24th of March was when the NATO aggression started against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and at the same time that was a sign that the terrorists should move towards the units of the army of Yugoslavia and MUP of Serbia. During that period, since Kotlina is in the border belt, to all intents and purposes, was where our combat group was, in-depth providing security for the border. And the terrorists set forth on an assault on Combat Group 3 with all -- they came out in all force to remove it from the positions, to inflict as much -- as many casualties as possible so that they could advance and then destroy -- to have the materiel and equipment destroyed by the NATO air force. The intervention unit, and I said a moment ago that every unit had an intervention unit, blocked the village of Kotlina straight away from the west and prevented them to take up their positions and inflicted casualties on terrorist forces located in Kotlina. When I say Kotlina, I don't mean the village of Kotlina, I mean the general area of Kotlina, and I've already said that was where the 162nd Terrorist Brigade was in operation from the Operative Group of Nerodimlje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, how did you acquire this information? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The figures, you mean. We didn't have the figures. We were just engaged in fighting combat with the terrorists. We didn't have the figures with us. Those figures and that information was the job of the MUP and verifiers. At this point in time the MUP. So our forces didn't enter the village. All they did was to block off --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How did you acquire the information about the incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's my unit. It was my unit. And when any event or incident takes place, the superior commander is informed, and then steps are taken to protect the unit straight away and then they report back to me, using a radio or a wire communication. In this case they let me know over the radio, radio connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, I thought the question was asking you to tell us what you knew of how the 12 KLA soldiers ended up in the wells.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army didn't enter Kotlina nor did it know about any wells. So we didn't enter Kotlina. All we did was to block the area off from the west. As to the number of casualties, I can see that from this here, and I heard on the basis of various reports in different newspaper articles and in this Tribunal here that there were a number of casualties. We did not know and could not know even an approximate number casualties because it's quite usual that the wounded and killed are taken away by the opposite side. That's what units do in combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps a striking feature of this case is that they weren't taken away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me repeat: We didn't enter the village of Kotlina, so we have no information as to how many victims or casualties there were in Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. I just wish to remind you that during the testimony of General Stevanovic here a whole set of photographs and photo documentation was provided, and in on-site investigation after the Kotlina incident, the number of weapons taken and the wells, which were not wells but the alleged wells because they were in fact shelters with a stove inside on an anti-terrorist operation, and for the record, I'd like it to be known or, rather, to object that Mr. Nice, as can be seen from this letter of his, knows full well that what we were dealing with here was the KLA. So we are wasting time talking about Kotlina as some civilians who fell casualty like in all other situations where it wasn't a question of civilians at all but it was combat against the KLA and that had that been properly investigated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 63 of the indictment -- just let me take a look. It's paragraph 63(k)(iv). It says this: "On or about the 25th of May, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked the village of Dubrava, municipality of Kacanik. During the attack, forces of the FRY and Serbia killed several Kosovo Albanian residents of Dubrava. Many residents of Dubrava formed a convoy of tractors and trailers and fled to Macedonia. Other residents fled to other villages or into forests before eventually crossing the border into Macedonia." That, then, is the 25th of May. Now, where is Dubrava or, rather, is Dubrava in your combat deployment?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is south of Urosevac, between Kacanik and Urosevac to the west, seven kilometres along the communication line between Urosevac, Doganovic and Globocica or, rather, the road leading to Strpce. It's at a crossroads there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mention is made of the 25th of May here. That's the date. So that's the time when your units were in the area, is it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the units were there before the 24th of March. That's where they were deployed. So this is if we can say halfway into the combat operations. And in this area or, rather, the region of Dubrava and Slatina-Vata-Doganovic is where there was a combat group or, rather, one unit, an armoured unit, artillery. That's it here. Here you have Dubrava. So that is where the Yugoslav army had its positions. I've already said that the army took up those positions in March. Through continuous action, the terrorists attacked the communication lines, wishing to cut across it, the Globocica-Urosevac road, to cut it off and cut off the units by the border and to prevent supplies from coming in and to force the unit to withdraw from its position. So the attacks were continuous on a column passing that way, rather, passing through Dubrava. Our columns during the war generally passed that way, and they were supply units, since the combat units were at their positions, and in view of the fact that the 243rd Mechanised Brigade over 80 per cent had tanks and APCs, that means they would have been detected straight away if they were to switch their motors on, and then destroyed. So the units, the supply units that were responsible for getting supplies to the front and in-depth, they moved along with security forces. As they were the target of terrorists attacks, the units for intervention and supplying security for the column intervened and fought the terrorists. Let me repeat: The army didn't enter any of the villages nor were there any attacks coming from the villages. The attacks took place outside the villages, 500 metres to one kilometre outside inhabited areas and settlements and that is because the configuration of the terrain is such that you were able to camouflage units and they knew that the army would react. So as not to suffer greater casualties along those communication lines, they would open fire from ambushes with several bursts of gunfire. As soon as the army would move to secure the column, they would just flee to the inhabited areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, General, in that area on the 25th of May, was there any other unit deployed there at all?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single unit. During that period, the period that you've just mentioned there was no unit during that period of time in my area of responsibility, that is to say you're probably thinking the villages Dubrava, Slatina, Doganovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean. Specifically I'm talking about Dubrava now, Dubrava and the area around the village of Dubrava, so not the village proper but the entire area surrounding the village. So you say there was no other unit there?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any police forces there?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was never there, never located there. The police had its own assignments. In addition to its regular assignments, its assignment was also to secure the communication lines, so it went along the communication lines and the roads, the main roads such as Urosevac-Kacanik, Urosevac-Doganovic or down to Globocica and Stimlje. Olup [phoen] was in Kacanik and in Strpce and in Urosevac as MUP. So not a single unit was located in that particular region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no police -- there were no police there in the area? It is the area of your combat deployment, the disposition of your unit, and that is two months into the aggression, you are at your own positions, and here it is being claimed that in fact some civilians fell casualty in Dubrava. Those are the charges. According to what you say, they could have fallen casualty only through the effects of your unit.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, in fighting my units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, was there any attack on the village at all? Not only on the 25th of May but generally speaking in that period of time from the time you took up your positions, which you say did you on the 24th of March. Was there any attack on the village at all?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of the brigade, and as you're looking at this particular section, there was no attack, nor was there any need for an attack on the village at all. The unit was at its positions in the areas around the village. As I've already said, you give three points to denote a region and the unit had taken up positions within that area. So if something were to crop up, you couldn't target your own region with artillery or tanks if the tanks were to shoot at your own positions. As you can see here, we had the artillery and armoured forces, so you can't target your own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you can -- have shown us, you see all this on your map; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's all on this map here. This area that I'm pointing to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was there any other unit in the area of Dubrava and Lisnaje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from my unit, there were no other units. So apart from the units of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade, there were no other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, now you were at that position and it was one of the axes of the ground aggression, the land aggression; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were fortified there with your artillery and your tanks. You were standing there in defence of your country, defending it against a land aggression; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For anybody to do anything, they would have to leave their tanks or their artillery pieces and go somewhere else, to a village, and mistreat the civilians and kill them. Is that what the situation would be?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. You see, the APCs don't have large crews. Three to four men manning a crew, depending on the type of tank. So to leave a tank on its own in order to go into a village to fight somebody over there with a rifle in your hands, I think that that was quite nonsensical. Nobody would do that because that would mean leaving the tank all on its own. And the tank couldn't move at all because it had to follow orders in view of the information that the AWACS were reconnoitering the area. So any -- not only movement of tanks but switching on the tanks' motors would have -- NATO would have detected the tanks through their heat devices, and the tanks would have been targeted and destroyed. So any movement was superfluous, and I'm talking about combat vehicles, heavy-duty vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand your 243rd Mechanised Brigade in fact has instruments of this kind, devices of this kind.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, according to its establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that an attack could have occurred, mounted by anybody at all, without your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility that was mine, during the aggression and before, there have been, according to the information we got from our security and intelligence organs and from the MUP, there have been attacks in -- even in villages where there was no army presence at all. That means that the terrorists had been conducting mobilisation by force or they settled accounts with some people in those villages, and we would find out very shortly, within 6 to 24 hours, that there were clashes in villages. Among them, in those villages where there was army presence nearby, there could not have been such conflicts because it was within our combat deployment area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far from Kotlina were your positions, the positions of your units?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have you moved from Dubrava to Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I mean Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dubrava is in fact in the area of defence of one of my units. In front of it, on the flank and in its rear, there are units. Dubrava itself is not within our combat deployment, because a combat deployment area never includes a populated area, only topographic features. So Dubrava was in one of the areas of one of the units. The attacks happened outside populated areas on open road so that, when fighting with terrorists begin -- begins, we never know where these people came from, and it's easier for them to flee to the mountains. You have to remember that this is a hilly, mountainous area, with Sar mountain nearby at a high altitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says that on or about the 25th of May, forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked the village of Dubrava. You say it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct because the army couldn't have attacked itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 66 -- 66(l) reads: "During the period between March 1999 and May 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia launched a series of massive offensives against several villages in the municipality of Kacanik, which resulted in the deaths of more than 100 civilians." So the period is March to May 1999. Could you tell us, please, from March to May 1999 and later, until the end of the war, your units were in the entire area of Kacanik municipality.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, then, where it says "... forces of the FRY and Serbia launched a series of massive offensives against several villages ..." is this correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. There was not a single offensive against a single village, literally speaking. We were subject to constant attacks, mostly in the border belt, during attempts to infiltrate enemy forces from the Republic of Macedonia, especially its western part. In the area of the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing, sometime early in May we were attacked by a group of 30, 40 terrorists who attacked an in-depth security detail. A staff sergeant of ours was killed then. Seven bodies of terrorists were later found. All border crossings were a daily permanent target of the terrorists who aimed to bring their forces into the FRY and have them linked up with the forces they already had on the territory of the FRY. I'm talking about the brigades of the KLA that I mentioned earlier; 161st, 62nd, and 63rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were no attacks against villages between March and May 1999.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there couldn't have been. We wouldn't have dared to mount any attacks, primarily because of the danger of the NATO aviation. At the same time, all the units had taken up their positions and put on camouflage in the third degree, and any movement would have resulted in huge losses on our side, except for intervention units that defended our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you have clarified Kotlina and the 24th of March. We won't dwell on it any longer. But there are several other points here. Under the same paragraph (l)(ii), it reads: "On or about the 13th of April, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded the village of Slatina and the hamlet of Vata. After shelling the village," it says, "infantry troops and police entered the village and looted and burnt the houses. During this action, 13 civilians were shot and killed." Do you know anything about these events? Please pay attention to the date, the 13th of April. On or about the 13th of April the village of Slatina, hamlet of Vata.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that part of the 162nd Terrorist Brigade was observing the area of the roads of Kacanik, Doganovic, and Globocica. Kacanik village is within the area -- sorry, the village of Slatina is within the area of defence, in the same area as the one where Dubrava is. Terrorist attacks from these so-called brigades were constant. This is the same road that I mentioned earlier. It goes from the forward positions of our unit to which supplies are brought of materiel and medical supplies. It was under constant attacks geared at cutting off the road. In the area of Slatina, not from Slatina village itself, these attacks could have been mounted. I am telling you again there could have been no action against the village because we were in the direct vicinity of those houses, those families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those positions were there from March?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says you surrounded Slatina and shelled it.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely this term "encirclement." If it is understood to mean occupying positions, going into position, then maybe a layman could call it that. We did move into position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In March. And you didn't leave them for a long time.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in those positions permanently from the 24th of March until the 12th or 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had been for 20 days, at least, in those positions by this date?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says from those positions you started firing at Slatina and hamlet of Vata and then went in to loot and burn.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We couldn't have shot at them. We couldn't have fired because we could have hit our own forces. Plus, it was mainly peaceful in those villages. We only suffered attacks on open roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not in villages?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Exclusively outside villages?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively outside populated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go into Slatina or Vata to do anything at all let alone loot and burn?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those villages, Dubrava that you mentioned earlier, Slatina and Vata, we never went into this because we didn't need to. It's not our job to search houses. It's the job of the MUP. We don't even have the authority to do that. So we didn't need to go in, not even to get supplies, because we had all we needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any firing from those positions?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By night. I have to say there are units that are on duty by night. One-third is always in position. If fire is opened at them from certain directions, which is a possibility, I cannot tell you from which directions, if volleys of fire target the positions, fire is returned. But the unit never moves from the line because the position they assume is a blocking defence position from which you don't move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Explain to me then why it wasn't [Realtime transcript read in error "was"] necessary for your forces to enter Dubrava, Slatina and Vata.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, what I said was that our forces did not enter those villages. They were in position. Positions are defined by points. They were the most favourable positions geographically speaking. You have points defining those positions on the left, right, and behind. Those were the best possible positions for organising armed struggle. So when you want to define a position, you don't mention a village, you say in the area of, and that's the broader area of a certain populated place. So our area is the road, is flanked by the road from Globocica to Doganovic. Lateral communications are almost impassable, especially in winter, and only communications from north to south were usable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question, Mr. Robinson, was why did the forces go into the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did your forces actually go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question was related to an answer given earlier that those villages, Dubrava, Slatina, and Vata, "we never went into because we didn't need to." So I asked him to explain why it wasn't necessary, why it wasn't necessary for his forces to enter those villages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want you to explain why it wasn't necessary for your forces to enter those villages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now the question is formulated quite differently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the decision that I issued, not a single unit needed to go into any village, including those three. There was no need because the unit was in position, completely equipped for combat, and there was nothing they needed to look for in villages. If resistance is offered or an attack is mounted against the unit, then they could respond, but they did not need to move from their positions, which are on the side of the populated areas. They didn't need to move into the populated area itself, because automatically they would fail to carry out their assignment if they went into villages. From houses they would be unable to perform their main task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But if they wanted to attack the village, to attack civilians in the village, presumably they would have to move into the village. Albeit, as you say, that would be in contravention of their orders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. If they had -- I don't know how you can put it that way, "if they had wanted to." Why would they go into the village? There was no reason for them to go into the village. We were there, that village was practically under our control. Every entry into a village implies normal presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you say the village was practically under your control.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How about that entire area in the area of deployment of your brigade? Was it under your control?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole area in the zone of the brigade within the demarcation lines under that tab that you asked me about was under our control, and I was responsible for the situation in the entire area of my responsibility. However, in that area of responsibility there were three terrorist brigades. They were not properly established army brigades, unlike the brigades of the army of Yugoslavia. Those were armed civilians, organised into informal groups and informal units; from three to five in smaller places, from 80 to 100 men in larger places. They moved around as civilians across the territory. The moment they would open fire from some direction or place, we would return fire. If we had reached that area, we would no longer find those armed people there, because by that time they would have discarded their weapons and uniforms and insignia or emblems, because they didn't have proper uniforms, and they would be dressed as civilians. The army did not have the authority or the capacity to investigate men that were blended with civilians. We didn't have time or authority to perform the paraffin glove test. All we could do was fight people who opened fire at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So was it possible for an incident of the kind that I just read out to you to happen in Vata on the 13th of April or around that date? Was it possible for somebody to barge into that village, to -- for police to come in and loot and burn? Was there any police there?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no police, and your unit did not have infantry.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had tanks and APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no police and no infantry because your unit was the only one there?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't shell any village?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been absurd to shell, because it was within our combat deployment. Shelling means the presence of tanks and heavy equipment with long range, and here we are talking about distances of up to 500 metres. So it would have been absurd to shell this populated area. It's impossible to use tanks to shell somebody with your own -- within your own combat deployment. It would have endangered your own men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So shelling was not possible. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, shelling was not possible within a populated area. What is possible is that terrorists from this village attacked army columns somewhere along this road going towards Doganovic, and it's possible they got killed in that fighting. It couldn't have happened in Dubrava, Slatina, or Vata, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I won't keep you on this issue any more. In this same paragraph under (iii), that's your territory as well, we read that: "On or about the 21st of May, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded the village of Stagovo. The population tried to escape towards the mountains east of the village. During this action, at least 12 persons were killed. Most of the village was looted and burnt down." Please indicate the location of Stagovo.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's above Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where the tip of the pointer was?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see on the map, Stagovo was between the positions of the units in Kacanik, the MUP forces in Kacanik, and my armoured detachment in the area of Stari Kacanik. It's a little to the west, three or four kilometres to the west. The army did not enter the village of Stagovo. What is characteristic of the village of Stagovo is that, from there, the terrorists, knowing there were strong forces in Kamena Glava, and probably having received instructions from the NATO alliance, they wanted to collect information about these units because these were the assault units of the brigade. So what they did was approach the positions by night and try to attack them. As the units had fortified their positions on time, the anti-armour detachment in March had fortified the positions, laid minefields in front and to the side for the protection of the anti-armour detachment, because the main purpose of this detachment was to fight tanks, so what it does is lay down minefields. When enemy forces come across the minefields, then they open fire on them. We experienced several attacks from the village of Stagovo. I know it was in May, but I can't recall the exact date. They attacked the anti-armour detachment in the area of Stari Kacanik two or three times, and also in the area of Kamena Glava. We knew about these attacks which were carried out by night. When we inspected the minefields in the morning, we found traces of blood, quite a lot of blood, pieces of clothing, but the bodies and the injured had been pulled out. The army never entered the village of Stagovo. The 3rd Brigade we mentioned, which had not been mobilised in 1998, had probably already mobilised and they were observing to the east of Kacanik and Urosevac. These were probably their members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're referring to a KLA brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you say about what it says here that the village of Stagovo was surrounded and the population tried to escape towards the mountains?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see on the map, we did not surround the village. We were practically to the west of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you'd been there for two months?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the 21st or 22nd of March. Some units were in this area where the Lepenac river runs. The eastern side is impassable. It's wooded, broken terrain, and the army couldn't be there. There was nothing for them to do there. So this village was never surrounded, especially not from the east, if holding positions means surrounding a village, and it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But was the village fired on from those positions?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were there any other units in this area?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Only your units?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No army units. There was only the MUP in Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no allegation, as I see it, in (iii) that the village was fired on. The allegation is that the village was surrounded. The population tried to escape, and then it says: "During this action -" it's not clear what that action is - "... 12 persons were killed." And then there is the allegation that the village was looted and burnt.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I appreciate what you say, but if it says that 12 persons were killed, they had to be killed by some kind of fire. That's why I put the question where the fire was opened. It says the village was looted and burnt. It was burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What can you say about that, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army did not enter the village, so it couldn't have either looted or burnt down the village. From 1998, all the orders given to the soldiers by the superior command and by me prohibited very strictly any entry into populated places or the taking of any kind of property. The movement of units towards the village of Stagovo would have meant abandoning their artillery pieces and their tanks. These were units consisting of small numbers of men, and it would have been absurd for them to cross the river Lepenac in that period. They would have had to use rafts in order to go and surround the village and open up fire. Who would then be looking after their artillery pieces? We didn't have the manpower to surround such villages, and it wasn't our job to do that. What I'm saying is that from these villages, probably - I can't be certain it's this village in particular, the village of Stagovo - but the terrorists went towards the units, approached the units by night and wandered into minefields. After two or three such incidents, they stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, I'll try to avoid putting a leading question. May I ask the usher to put this map, which was admitted into evidence during the testimony of General Djosan, where the parts of the territory under attack by NATO have been marked. And could you indicate on this map the combat disposition of your brigade.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat disposition of the brigade was as follows: This was the combat disposition of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where are the villages I have just quoted, mentioned?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to stand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can compare the two maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is Stagovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's Stagovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is Stagovo. Is Slatina nearby?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where is Slatina? Where is Dubrava? Where is Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's on the border?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the border belt. Dubrava, Slatina, Doganovici. The map is on a large scale, so some hamlets are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, how intensive was the bombing of the combat deployment of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a barracks to the west of Urosevac, about two kilometres away, and over 220 projectiles were fired on that barracks alone during the aggression. About 400 projectiles were fired in the area of responsibility of the brigade, and you can see part of it here. I didn't have this map, so I couldn't carry out an analysis, but you can see where most of the firing on the units of my brigade took place. Mostly it was around Urosevac, on the Stimlje-Dulje road. So these were the two axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When Stagovo is mentioned here, there is also a mention of looting, looting and burning down. Did you have any instances of looting in your unit?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single soldier or officer committed a crime during the aggression or before that without this being discovered. There were individual instances. The numbers were insignificant. I think there were ten or 12 persons in the brigade who were charged with crimes such as taking property from abandoned houses. There was no organised criminal activity, no organised looting, especially because in each area and on each of the axes I mentioned we had military police searching literally all the men passing through the area, whether coming or going. They controlled the situation to make sure that nobody took anything away from the area. And this also applied to the area of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on, then. Under (iv), and all this refers to Kacanik, Kotlina, Slatina, Stagovo, Dubrava, Lisnaje. "On or about the 25th of May," it says here, you surrounded the village of Dubrava "... the population was ordered to gather at the school and leave the village on tractors. Men were then separated from women and children. During this action four men were killed. In addition, four members of the Qorri family were killed while trying to escape towards the woods." I have quoted this passage. What do you know about it? We are now talking about the 25th of May. Were there any other units in that area on the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have already mentioned the 25th of May. There was no expelling people from houses, making them go to a school. In the areas of defence of the units, I was informed of every incident. I'm referring to the areas of the subordinate units. Had such things happened, I'm sure I would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this is a major incident. The population was ordered to gather at the school, to leave the village on tractors. Did you force the population of Dubrava to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never issued any orders to expel civilians from houses, to organise convoys, to have the population go on tractors or any other vehicles anywhere. For the most part people left out of fear, and this was quite logical. When they saw a build-up of troops, they expected that there would be aggression on these axes. They were familiar with the terrain, they expected the NATO forces to come from the south, and probably for this reason the population not just of these villages but elsewhere, whoever had relatives in Macedonia or in other areas, they went to Macedonia. Many Serbs went there because they had families there. We didn't prevent people from leaving, but we only directed them not to go where there was combat deployment or where there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Here we have the same pattern that has already been repeated many times. It says: "Men were then separated from women and children." Did any of your units ever engage in any such activities like separating men from women and children?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From March 1998 until June 1999, not for a single moment in a single unit was there any separation by gender or by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that four people were killed. Were you ever in Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Doganovic was my command post. It says on the map 243, and there was a tank there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 243 means the command post of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the command post. Before that, in 1998, we had been in the Banjica area and I mentioned there was a military police battalion there which was under my command in 1998. In the area of Doganovici and the area of Banjica, and that's about three kilometres to the west. We knew that there would be a breakthrough here or, rather, that this command post would be discovered. There was factory there, and I proposed to the corps command, and they agreed, that I should go to Urosevac and that the command should be where there was the focus of combat activities and that the forward command post should be in Rankovici and Globocica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's conclude with the events in Dubrava according to what it says here in paragraph 66(l)(iv). Could anything like this have happened without your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite certain that it couldn't have happened without my knowledge, because it would have been absurd. Perhaps due to communications something might have been overlooked or neglected. Because of interference, because of power cuts, communications might be late a few hours, but an incident of this kind could not have occurred without my knowledge as the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So any incident where somebody was killed you would have had to have known about?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, every incident, and especially if someone was killed, a soldier or civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, paragraph 105 of the indictment related to Kosovo, it says that the -- "In addition to the forced expulsions of Kosovo Albanians, forces of the FRY and Serbia also engaged in a number of killings of Kosovo Albanians ... Such killings occurred at numerous locations, including" among other things, Kacanik. So that is your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what can you tell us about that, these allegations here that killings occurred of Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of any Albanians being killed in Kacanik, no killings. The MUP was in Kacanik throughout, and it's a small town which was under our control, that is to say the control of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. All I know is that there were two incidents that occurred there in the Kacanik area sometime towards the end of February, I think it was the 28th of February, when a captain was killed - I think I mentioned this - and four other policemen wounded. And on the 7th or 8th of March, there was an attack on the patrol where 8 policemen were wounded. The MUP sought -- engaged in a search to find the terrorists. They fought the terrorists for a night and a day and fought them up in the mountains around Kacanik to uncover the perpetrators. There were no other killings. The citizens were in Kacanik. They went about their daily lives and business. Life evolved normally since it is a place in the municipality. The army did not enter the place at all nor did it have any need to. The army was at its positions outside Kacanik. It did not enter the municipality of Kacanik at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We heard testimony here from Isufu Loku from Kacanik, and he said that on the 8th and 9th of March, 1999, the Serb forces attacked Kotlina and that he saw members of the army and MUP entering the village with tanks and that on the occasion 17 people in the village were burnt to death, during the night a number of people disappeared, and this witness afterwards found the bodies of two locals from Kotlina. So he is referring to the 8th and 9th of March 1999. Do you know anything at all about that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th and 9th of March is when the verifiers were still there. They had information. Let me repeat: The army did not enter Kotlina, and from the area of Kotlina Combat Group 3 was attacked. So not the village but the area around. The army did not enter the Kotlina area, nor do I have any knowledge of any killings at all - whether it be two or four, that's not important - or that there was destruction and burning and looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what he says, is that correct or not correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He said that on the 24th of March, he's now referring to the 24th of March, and the verifiers weren't there then, it was just your units that were there?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He says they attacked the village of Kotlina again and he and his relatives took to the mountains, a mountain called Sesic, or something like that, I don't know how it's pronounced and whether you've heard of it, but he saw tanks and fire coming from the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that we didn't move the tanks at all. We didn't enter the village. And on the 24th of March, the other villages, Junsevo, [phoen] Palivo [phoen], Denica, Pustenik, Krivenik [phoen], those other villages, there was an all-out attack launched on units that were in the first belt or, rather, providing in-depth security. If there were any casualties, they were casualties that occurred during combat up towards Golemo Brdo or Belo Brdo, those hills. And if you look at the tanks and you analyse the communication lines in this area, it is early spring we're talking about in this area, which means the slopes of Mount Sara, you have communication lines at an altitude of over a thousand metres, and there are no roads -- no asphalt roads. You can't use the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at his own map. If he wants us to follow it, he'll have to point to the one on the easel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Point to the map on the easel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Explain what you're indicating.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the village of Kotlina from which there was constant attacks on Combat Group 3. As it is stated there, that tanks entered the village. Just take a look for yourselves. Look at the communication lines and both the roads. These two were passable, however, the lateral communications were completely or almost impassable during that time of year because you're talking about the regions about -- around Mount Sarina where the altitude is from 900 metres to over a thousand metres there. Village roads, rural roads. So faced with a situation like that when you had absolute supremacy in the air, to leave your positions and move your tanks two or three kilometres and then come back, that would be absurd. It would be tantamount to self-destruction, suicide. The units that engaged in battle with terrorists from Kotlina were certain units engaged in anti-terrorist operations, and I said that each unit had its own assignment. They are rapid deployment units with PRDs and Pragas, and they were able to move quickly and resist the enemy for several hours and then withdraw again, change their positions, and avoid possible NATO strikes, NATO Air Force strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here before me a report on the -- technical report from the municipality of Kacanik, village of Kotlina. It is dated the 24th of March, 1999. The participants were terrorists unknown. That's what it says in the report of the Secretariat of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we have a reference, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we place this on the overhead projector and you can look at it. We're not going to dwell on this document, just this portion. It is tab 212, Stevanovic, and 213 during General Stevanovic's testimony. You can just look through it briefly. That's the 24th of March. 24th of March, crime-scene investigation. And in line 2 of the text?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Kacanik 1999. Participants: Terrorists unknown, described in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this document just to refresh your memory. What is it -- what does it say in the underlined portions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we don't have the English version with us here. We'll have to send for it. Having had a look at the document, it may make more sense if the English version goes on the overhead projector to assist the Chamber, if the accused has got it with him as he should do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you going to make much use of this document, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. You don't need an English version for the photographs. But what I want him to read, well, the interpreters can translate that. It's just a few words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, General, you were looking at a printed text, typed out. Do you have it on the overhead projector?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, go back to that page. Not the report. You have two portions which were underlined. Just a moment ago you were looking at that portion. Have you seen the underlined portions?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says, "One of the bodies discovered." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says, "shelter in the form of a well."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "One the corpses was found and photographed close to a shelter in the form of a well."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does it say in the second sentence?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Yes. It shows corpses found above the village of Kotlina in another shelter or well."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, was this house burned down? Has it been burnt down?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. This house hasn't been set fire to or burnt down. You can see the doors, the windows, the fence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we looked at all those pictures with Stevanovic. What's the point of repeating all these?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the point of it is that it is precisely in that area that the unit of General Jelic was located, and he is explaining to us what happened on the occasion, and he just is confirming what General Stevanovic said about that particular subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but he's doing it by reading something that's already been read to us. What's the point in that? It doesn't add a thing to the evidence we've already heard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it's quite clear that these exhibits in fact prove that absolute -- there was absolutely nothing here to do with any crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's for us to decide. Move on to another matter, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that same witness, Isufu Loku, said that he heard from Zymeri about a massacre of 22 young men killed by the Serb forces with an explosion, explosive. Do you know anything about any massacre in Kotlina, et cetera, or the event that was before you? And actually, you only know about things indirectly.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of a massacre or this mass killing, which that would have been. Had any killing like that taken place, or even close to that scale of killing, I would certainly know about that. Now, to kill them with an explosion, well, I don't know what this term means. How can you kill someone with an explosion? There can be casualties, but how can you kill 20 people by some sort of explosion? But perhaps there's an error in terms, but anyway, I haven't heard of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness K31 from Kacanik, a protected witness, no name, she said that on the 24th of May, that is to say that same date is referred to -- no, this is the 24th of May, I'm sorry. In the transcript it is 8130 is the page number. She said that -- the witness was herself from Kacanik. She said that an explosion woke them up, an explosion near her mother's house, and in a group of 16 they set off in the direction of the mountain. Now, what was happening? Was there an explosion on the 24th of May in Kacanik at all?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of May, whether there was an explosion that day and what time, I really can't remember that. There were very frequent explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that was during the NATO bombing, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially when there was an airstrike on the part of NATO. So there were explosions on a daily basis, hundreds of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, she said she was woken up by one such explosion.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and she went to the -- took to the forest and then went to Macedonia. So all of us were woken in the area by the NATO aggression and the explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, she does say, truth to tell, that in a group of 16 they set out in the direction of the mountain and that the remainder of the group stayed in the forest and the Serb forces drew close to them and then shot at the group but there were no wounded. That's what she says. So that's not the important part, but anyway, she says she was woken up by the explosion. You say you were all woken up by the explosion.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't sleep for days and nights. Not only her and in Kacanik but in all the surrounding villages because the explosions. You can hear an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You indicated on Djosan's map the density of the bombing of your area of defence, so I don't suppose that is being challenged, that there were there these explosions which could be heard. Were there bombings every day or were there breaks and pauses in the bombing when there were no NATO airstrikes?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that for 90 per cent of the time there were bombings and explosions, because Urosevac is where the overall area of responsibility is to be found and it is along a corridor which stretched from Macedonia or, rather, Greece, Macedonia towards the interior of Serbia and Kosovo. So there was bombing almost every day. Sometimes there were 50 projectiles in just one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, the witness Fadil Vishi testified about the events in the village of Dubrava in the Kacanik municipality. Let's see what he says. He said that on the 25th of May he was watching from the forest and saw Serb forces stopping a convoy of peasants who were endeavouring to leave Dubrava, and they arrested six persons. What can you tell us about that? What do you have to say? That means you are those forces that he's talking about which, on the 25th of May 1999, as you said, there were no nobody else except your forces there, so what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was nobody there. First of all, the army didn't stop anyone, ask for identification papers, or keep them and separate them in any way. The army had orders in 1998 and 1999 that all persons moving along the communication lines, let me repeat, should be directed to safe areas. So that if there were combat in the region, to avoid these people from being casualties and the targets of any attack, either our forces or terrorist forces. But they directed them to secure and safe places and in the direction they wished to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, General. But let's just clear one thing up. He said under oath -- and it is 4448 page of the transcript, the 7th of May is when he testified, 2002. He said that he, on the 25th of May, watched from the forest and saw Serb forces stopping a convoy of peasants trying to leave Dubrava and that they arrested six persons. Therefore, we have established here through your answers that there were no other forces on that particular day or around that time of the 25th of May except your own forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, if he says he saw a convoy stopped by what he refers to as Serb forces and arrested six people, they must have been your forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me this: Did you indeed stop any convoy of peasants leaving Dubrava and did you arrest anyone?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be practical. Possibly that the first two or three vehicles stopped, as is wont to happen, to see whether they can go on. So you would have to stop and ask the way, and the commanding officer will say, yes, you can move ahead, you can take that such-and-such direction, north or south or whatever, and then the column would pass by or, rather, the people would leave. We had no right to arrest anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's leave that aside that you didn't have the right to do that, but did it -- anything happen? Did -- was anybody taken into custody or detained?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if they had on them insignia or weapons. Then that kind of person would be detained and -- but there were no searches or anything like that. Nobody was detained. Nobody was searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell us something of the circumstances that prevailed in the area, because this particular witness, the one I quoted a moment ago, on that same page of the transcript goes on to say that from January 1999 Dubrava was isolated, that there were no telephone communications and no electricity. January 1999.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he's partially right on that score. You know very well that from the beginning of March and -- or, rather, until the beginning of March, the whole system functioned properly because it functioned in the state. However, at the end of March or, rather, from the 24th of March, after the NATO airstrikes, the telecommunications systems were destroyed and the transformer stations and Urosevac as a town itself throughout the war didn't have even 30 per cent of the electrical energy it usually had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he says from January 1999 Dubrava was isolated, no telephone communications or electricity.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the villages did have those -- did have electricity and telephones until the aggression started or, rather, nobody had telephones except for 30 telephone numbers as of the 25th of March. The post office was destroyed. We used the old exchange. We linked it to the railway station and were able to communicate with the superior command, and we gave a few telephone numbers to the organs of power and authority, to the authorities, not to leave them without any communication whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the -- and the General, the interpreters are asking you to slow down, but we'll take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's move ahead quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As fast as I can, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Muharem Dashi spoke about Stagovo, about incidents of the 21st and 22nd of May, 1999. That is the time when your unit was the only one there; correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, he says that he saw men moving on foot towards Stagovo. I have a brief summary of his testimony. Sometime at 4.15, he says, he was unable to see civilians, but he says they were surrounded by paramilitaries. Could you please tell us whether in Stagovo or elsewhere in your area of responsibility there were any paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of the brigade, in the defence area and in the area of Stagovo, there were never any paramilitaries, nor was there any paramilitary unit ever in the area of the defence of the brigade. The only paramilitaries were the Siptar terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He says also, among other things, that when the army or, rather, the Serbian forces left the village, he went back to the village and saw that 90 per cent of the houses were burnt down, as well as barns, that houses were looted, and the doors on the mosque and the schoolhouse were broken down and even some animals were killed. He said all that testifying here.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information, nor did I ever have such information. If that had happened, if that had been committed by my unit or the neighbouring unit in the vicinity of Stagovo, I would have known about it. So it certainly wasn't done by the army. Plus, the army had never entered the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He even says that there were several dead people there and that his cousin buried them on the 22nd of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about any casualties in Stagovo except those that I mentioned earlier that advanced towards the anti-armour detachment and came across minefields.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sejdi Lami, from Kacanik, said here that on the 14th of May, villagers of Lata -- do you know of such a village, Lata?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a village didn't exist. He probably means Vata.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could be. They left the village after an attack on the 13th of May and that they were stopped on the way to Macedonia by Serb forces who wanted money from them in exchange for safe passage. He testified on the 6th of May, 2002, page 4396 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's probably -- he was probably in the area of those three villages and hamlets. They did move towards the border, but the army didn't stop anyone, they didn't ask for their IDs or money. That was not their job. Plus, the army was in their trenches, manning their equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you leave the village of Vata to go towards the border, which route would you take? Could you show us on the map.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here is the village of Vata.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that's Vata. Where would they go if they wanted to go to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could go towards Globocica. That's the shortest route. And the other possibility is the route via Kacanik towards Djeneral Jankovic and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But whichever route they took, they would go through the combat deployment of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They would go through the combat deployment of Combat Group 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who could have stopped them on the way, asking for money or whatever?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were parts of our brigade there. Nobody could have stopped them except for terrorists or gangs of criminals who seemed to be always present in such situations. It's possible that they did that. The only authorities who could have inspected their documents, meaning IDs and driving licenses, were MUP organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any MUP there?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not here, only at the border crossing, not on the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was no police there, only on the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on the border crossing. Or perhaps if there was an intervention action, the MUP would be defending the road or defending themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know maybe if Vata was a terrorist stronghold of some kind, because he says that some KLA soldiers were housed in a house in Vata which they left on the 12th of April already, and he was testifying about an attack on the 13th of May. Was there a terrorist group in Vata?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In one of your earlier questions you mentioned the 13th of April, and now you mentioned the 12th of April in Vata.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. He said that those KLA members left the house in Vata on the 12th of April, and he testified at the same time that on the 14th of May - that is a month later - the villagers left Vata due to a Serb attack that happened on the 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in this area, in view of the importance of this road, there were terrorist groups all the time that ran to and fro between combat deployment areas of various units. It was our estimate that there were 150 to 200 terrorists in this area. That's one battalion from the 162nd KLA brigade. They were constantly along this road, and they would make occasional incursions. It was mainly men from these villages in the area of the road from Doganovic via Slatina towards Globocica. Those were members of the 162nd Brigade of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This witness said that on the 13th of April four Pragas and six trucks with 100 regular soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia shelled the village, resulting in the villagers fleeing towards the mountains. Tell me, is it true that on the 13th of April this happened, resulting in the death of 13 civilians?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you already the reasons why no village was shelled. To the right of Vata and in front of Vata there were combat positions of our units. So there was no shelling and no combat activity in these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isa Raka, a witness from Kacanik, transcript page 4359, testified on the 2nd of May, 2002, said that on the 2nd of May Serb forces --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, Serb forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I've asked you to move ahead quickly, but bear in mind the interpreters. They're asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You heard what the witness said, that Serb forces attacked Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard. Kacanik is a municipality under our control. Our authorities were in charge and all state authorities were operating. The army never attacked Kacanik nor did it ever have any reason to, and they never entered Kacanik. This witness says he was in the woods, waiting for two days. He was probably waiting for somebody to take him across. How could we know who was where, waiting to cross the border? The border is to be crossed at legal border crossings, not through woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Hazbi Loku, a witness from Kacanik, Kotlina village, stated here that on the 24th of March, the village was surrounded by Serb forces, that they entered houses, took villagers away towards the centre of village, including women and children. They asked for valuables to be turned over. Men had to lay down on the ground. The villagers were transported by truck to the village of Lac. Military trucks -- it says you took them away in military trucks on the 24th and 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army never entered Kotlina, nor did it have any direct contact with civilians. You can see from this this is pure fabrication, a lie. Look at the map. Kotlina and Lac, it's just one kilometre away on the road. I don't know if I can show you here. Right. This is Kotlina. Look. It's one centimetre on the map. It is approximately one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Kilometre where?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kilometre on the road. The distance which the children and women were transported across.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He claims that you transported them to the village of Lac by trucks and then they went on on foot to Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our vehicles were full of food and ammunition. Imagine us unloading ammunition, going two or three kilometres from our position to that village to transport somebody across a distance of 500 metres to one kilometre, and then letting them walk on for ten kilometres more. I think it is complete nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This witness said that in Ivaja on the 8th of March, 1999, the mosque was destroyed. Do you know anything about an incident in Ivaja on the 8th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Ivaja, on the 8th of March, if my memory serves me right, MUP forces were active, and I think it was stated here already that this action happened after a commander was killed in Kacanik. There was no army in Ivaja. There were gather groups further down, providing in-depth security of the border. MUP, in the course of this action, entered Ivaja looking for perpetrators of this crime, and the army only raised its level of alertness and put up defences to the west of Ivaja. Therefore, the army didn't go into the village and I have no information if anything was destroyed or looted because the army never went in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the 8th of March. Verifiers were there. All right. Then on the 9th of March, he says, Serb forces blocked Kacanik. The people were sent -- were actually moving towards the border but the authorities turned them back, and some people disappeared on the 9th of March. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th of March is the date when verifiers were still there. Our units were to the left and right of the cross -- of the border crossing. The army does not hold the border crossing. It is held by the MUP. The army never expelled anybody towards Macedonia, never checked anybody's papers or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Milosevic. No translation is coming across in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, continue. Perhaps you would repeat that. You should repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So paragraph 63(j). I am charged with the fact that in Urosevac municipality, which was the seat, the base of your brigade ...

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And also the command of the garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were a garrison commander in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in Urosevac, during the period between the 24th of March and the 14th of April, that means the first 20 days of the war, "... forces of the FRY and Serbia shelled and attacked villages in the Urosevac municipality, including the villages of Biba, Muhadzer Prelez, Raka, and Staro Selo, killing a number of residents. After the shelling, forces of the FRY and Serbia entered some of the villages, including Papaz and Sojevo, and ordered the residents to leave. Other Kosovo Albanians from Varos Selo and Mirosavlje fled their villages as the Serb forces entered. After the residents left their homes, the soldiers and policemen burned the houses. The displaced persons went to the town of Urosevac where most boarded trains which carried them to the Macedonia border crossing at Djeneral Jankovic. Serb forces directed the train passengers to walk on the railroad tracks to the border. Others travelled in convoys ..." and their documents were confiscated. What can you say about these allegations in the indictment from the 24th of March to the 14th of April? Before you answer that, could you show us on the map these villages: Biba, Muhadzer Prelez, Raka, Staro Selo.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Biba. Staro Selo, Muhadzer and Trnovace, Muhadzer Prelez, Sojevo, Mirosavlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Mirosavlje. All these villages mentioned here are to the east and south of Urosevac for the most part.
